steps.action:
The lighthouse had been automated for ten years before Elias arrived, which meant his job, on paper, didn’t exist.

The town council called him a “heritage caretaker.” The Coast Guard called him “the old man up there.” The tourists who pointed phone cameras from the ferry called him nothing at all; he was just a small figure on the gallery, a rust-colored jacket against a white tower, as decorative as the railing.

Elias preferred “keeper.” Someone had to keep things.

The lamp still worked, though now it hummed with electronics and never faltered unless the grid did. The rotating lens, a century-old Fresnel assembly that had once been polished with whale oil and rags, gleamed behind glass. Technicians came once a year with laptops and plastic cases, checked terminals, ticked boxes, left.

Between those visits, the tower belonged to Elias.

In the mornings, he climbed the spiral of iron steps to the lantern room. His boots knew every rung, every spot where the paint had blistered. The sea pushed itself against the rocks below, sending up the same chill breath it had exhaled on his father and his grandfather, both of whom had been keepers when the light was still a living thing that needed hands.

He wiped away salt crust that the wind had thrown against the windows overnight. No one had asked him to. No one paid him for polish or pride. But the salt dulled the glass and blurred the beam, even if modern regulations said the radar and GPS were what mattered now.

“Light’s a promise,” his grandfather had once told him, sitting in the old watch room with a mug of black coffee. “Ships don’t always keep their machines running. But they look for the promise.”

Standing in that same room, Elias could still smell that coffee sometimes, even though he now drank tea.

At night, the lamp cycled with patient precision, an automated guardian casting its white sweep over the black water. Elias would sit at the desk below, making entries in a logbook no one had required for years: weather, wind, wave height, passing vessels, curious birds, a broken shutter hinge, the name of a trawler that had passed too close for his comfort.

On a Tuesday in late October, a storm came in crossing two directions—a bruise-purple wall on the horizon in the afternoon, turning the sea to hammered iron. The forecast called it “severe but routine.” The town adjusted lawn chairs and tucked away hanging plants. The last ferry left early.

Elias watched from the gallery. The air thickened; gulls fled inland. The hairs on his arms rose as static crawled over the metal rail.

Routine, he thought, is just catastrophe that’s done this before.

The wind hit in the evening, smearing rain sideways like icy ropes. The lighthouse shuddered, a solid old animal bracing against the weather. Lights along the little harbor flickered. Then, all at once, the shore went black.

Outage, Elias realized. Transmission lines down.

The lamp above him did not flicker. The lighthouse had its own backup generators, tested monthly by some invisible schedule in a central office. The beam continued to turn, faithful and insistent.

He could have stayed indoors. The systems would run themselves. That was the assumption baked into the word “automated.” Instead, habit tugged him up the stairs.

He checked the generator by the tight white light of his headlamp. Fuel lines, voltage, temperature—numbers steady and good. He confirmed the control panel’s status, the steady green of functioning systems. The lamp’s motor purred like a cat in the gale.

On the third pass of the beam he saw it: a shadow where no shadow should be, low on the horizon, briefly carved out of the night. A vessel, lights down, moving wrong—closer to the off-shore rocks than any chart recommended.

Elias went to the old radio console, the one the technicians had eyed with condescension and left in place only because removing it would have cost more than ignoring it. He flipped the switches. Relays clicked reluctantly to life.

“Unidentified vessel three miles east of Whitecap Light,” he said into the microphone, voice steady from the muscle memory of decades. “You are approaching dangerous submerged rocks. State intentions.”

Static answered him, thick as wool.

He repeated the call, then again, altering his phrasing, the way his father had taught him: not accusing, not panicked. Clear. Precise. More static.

The radar, an aging green eye, painted a blip sliding toward the spray of pale fuzz that marked shoals. No AIS signal, no transponder data. A dark ship in a dark storm, heading where steel and stone would meet.

He leaned closer to the window, wiping away condensation. Another sweep of the beam revealed the vessel more clearly this time—a small freighter, he judged, deck sometimes vanishing completely between waves.

“Unidentified freighter east of Whitecap,” he said, putting iron into his words. “Alter course ten degrees starboard immediately. You are on a collision path with submerged hazard.”

The static cracked, then thinned. A hesitant voice bled through, accented and strained. “…whitecap station… instruments… not reliable… we see no hazard.”

Of course they saw nothing. Their radar was likely washed with rain; their charts probably older than the paint on their hull.

“Trust the light, captain,” Elias said. “My bearings: you are three minutes from disaster. Turn starboard ten degrees. I will maintain visual.”

Silence, except for distant shouting beneath the open mic. The lighthouse vibrated as a particularly vicious gust slammed into it. For a moment, the beam’s rotation stuttered, slowed, then resumed.

“Three minutes,” Elias repeated. “Turn now.”

On the radar, the blip hesitated. To anyone else, it might just have been noise, a quiver in the signal. To Elias, who had watched such screens and seas for a lifetime, it was a decision being made out there in the dark.

Then the blip shifted. A slow, grudging curve.

Through the glass he caught the freighter’s flank taking the waves at a different angle. The storm swallowed details immediately, but he knew what he’d seen. The ship’s bow, adjusted by that thin slice of degrees, would now slide along the safe side of the rocks, like a coin passing the edge of a drain.

He stayed at the window, breath fogging the glass, until the radar showed the vessel moving steadily north, away from the danger. When he raised the microphone again, his hand had begun to shake, though from cold or adrenaline he couldn’t say.

“Alteration acknowledged,” the captain’s voice came, clearer than before. “We… did not expect manual…” The sentence crumbled under a crackle. Then: “Thank you, Whitecap. We would not have seen.”

Elias looked up at the light. It revolved, serene as a planet, washing the rain with its exact intervals.

“Keep to your new heading,” he said. “Whitecap out.”

He shut down the radio, feeling the storm pressing against the tower, the way grief had pressed against him years ago when automation first came and his father’s post was declared obsolete. The world had decided they didn’t need keepers anymore—that circuits and backups and regulations made them redundant.

Maybe they were right, almost all of the time.

He descended to the watch room, picked up his pen, and opened the logbook. The page for that day already held notes about wind direction, barometric pressure, the first sighting of migrating geese. He added a line in his small, careful hand:

“2117 hrs – Assisted unidentified freighter in altering course from shoals during grid outage. Light and radio functioning nominal. Promise kept.”

He paused, then underlined the words once.

By morning, the storm had blown itself into tatters. The town’s power returned, the shoreline lights winking back to life one by one. People would speak of fallen branches, of trash cans overturned and shingles lost. The freighter would pass beyond the horizon, cargo intact, crew telling a brief, half-believed story of a voice on the radio and a beam in the rain.

Tourists came again a few days later, pointing cameras from the ferry. In their photos, the lighthouse stood as always, white against blue, the little figure on the gallery just part of the scene. Automated. Decorative.

Inside, Elias checked the generator, logged the storm, and polished the panes of the lantern room until the glass vanished and the light seemed to float in the air, clean and bright.

Someone had to keep things, even the things that now kept themselves.

As the sun slid down and the first ship of the evening winked its mast light on the horizon, the lamp began its night’s rotation. Its beam turned, unblinking, sweeping across familiar water and unknown hulls.

It was more than illumination, Elias thought, listening to the quiet machinery hum. It was the old promise his grandfather had spoken of, made by steel and glass instead of hands, but a promise all the same: You are not alone out there. Someone is watching.

Keeper and light, each in their way, keeping watch over the other.
